To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a model bird alula, whose area is 1% that of the wing it is mounted on, can stabilize an attached vortex on a thin, unswept wing.

the bird's alula stabilizes an attached leading-edge vortical flow on the outer hand wing at post-stalling angles of attack by merging otherwise separated vortical flows from the wing's leading and side edges.
the alula’s role in the generation and maintenance of an attached LEV is to merge otherwise separate leading-edge and side-edge vories.

how a bird’s outer hand wing and alula work together to generate lift.
the aerodynamics of birds’ wings.
the flow physics of a bird’s wing and how it may be used to improve the flight performance of unmanned aerial vehicles.

a bird’s alula is a key contributor to the maintenance of an LEV over its thin-profiled outer hand wing.
the model alula, which is a small winglet, stabilizes an attached LEV on a wing by merging otherwise separate leading- & side-edge vortices.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a bird’s alula is a vortex steering mechanism that stabilizes a recircular aft-tilted leading-edge vortex on a thin wing at post-stoll angles of attack.
the alula is a leading-edge vortex stabilizer.
birds can generate an attached LEV on their wing by using an alula to steer the leading edge vorticity and generate a wall jet.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the alula is a vortex steering mechanism.
a thin, streamwise-extending structure can stabilize an aft-tilted vortex over the leading edge of an otherwise unswept wing.

the LEV is a key element in bird alula function, and that its stability can be attributed to a combination of two flow phenomena: the steering of spanwisely generated vorticity back to the wing and the aft-tilting and outboard evacuation of LEV vortical flow.
